30 Years of Democracy - South Africa as our home

By: Marion Edmunds | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africans reflect on how the democratic South Africa has served them as their home over the last thirty years

Unique Selling Point:
We have a unique opportunity to feel the pulse of South Africa's democracy through the lived experience of a range of people across South Africa. This is a story about South Africa and her people: A reflection on how we are doing, what brought us to this point and how do we feel about the future.

Summary:
The history of SA is one of migration, displacement, belonging, exile, leaving home to seek new opportunities elsewhere. So our focus will be on the landscape and the different challenges experienced by the citizens of five of our main provinces.

We propose dividing the 72 minute documentary into six parts (of about 12 minutes each), with an introduction and conclusion making up one part, and five longer parts where we get to know people who have been part of the democratic journey in different areas of the country, but who we find in their homes.

To develop a picture of that journey we propose to separate each part or segment with poetic visuals – drones, wide shots, close up shots, stills, time lapses – of transport infrastructure: roads, railways, runways, traffic, taxis, cars, aeroplanes, potholes, broken bridges, contrasting both the sophisticated infrastructure that works and that which is broken. The images will also speak to what binds us, what connects us to the landscape. Much of this will be without voice over or narrative and will paint a verbal picture. They will also provide a dynamic tension with the homes we visit.

We will need to film in both rural and urban spaces, across five provinces - Gauteng, Eastern Cape, Western Cape, Kwazulu-Natal and maybe Northern Cape.

In locating our characters at home, we will also, by default, highlight the issues of migration, and displacement, isolation, belonging, disillusionment, loss, hope and love which are also common in the country’s experience. The infrastructure segways will contribute to that effect.

We propose a narrative voice to link the parts but will keep the wording sparse. It will be a voice to link and create context rather than an explaining voice.

We will focus the interview on three main questions:
1) How are you feeling about South Africa as your home?
2) What events have happened to make you feel like that?
3) What are your hopes for the future South Africa?

Those questions will be set in an interview which also asks them questions about who they are and how they live their life. The answers will be threaded through the documentary with broader context provided by political and social experts. The characters and experts selected will be given licence to answer in seriousness but also with humour. We hope to interview approximately three to four people and expert in each province, with some specifically identified for a slightly different Afrikaans version.

Explore 30 Years of Democracy with Carte Blanche

M-Net celebrates Freedom Day with the broadcast of a 90-minuted Carte Blanche special, looking back at three decades of democracy in South Africa, on Sunday 28 April at 7pm. 30 Years of Democracy tells the story of South Africa and her people, from the moment democracy was attained, , reflecting on the journey so far and imagining what the perfect destination looks like.

Thirty years after the country’s first free, fair, democratic election in 1994, the Carte Blanche team travels across South Africa to meet people from all walks of life, sharing their realities, hearing their dreams and listening intently to their hopes for the future. Rather than being a history of post-apartheid South Africa or apolitical assessment of South Africa’s destiny,, 30 Years of Democracy seeks to gain an understanding of how South Africans have experienced the last thirty years living in this country, how it has shaped their identity and whether they believe their hopes, wants and needs will be realised in the future

“The Carte Blanche team takes to the highways, streets and back roads to speak to South Africans from all walks of life in their homes: from a Sandton chef to a rural chief, a Durban Street artist to a medical student, and a lawyer to a taxi boss,” says Waldimar Pelser, Channel Director: Premium Channels at MultiChoice. “We think we know South Africa because we live the everyday realities – but how often do we consider the lived experience of a wider cross-section of the country and seek to understand what people’s hopes for their country are?”

The history of SA is one of migration, displacement, belonging, exile and leaving home to seek new opportunities elsewhere. It’s also one of resilience and solidarity. 30 Years of Democracy focuses on the landscape and the different challenges experienced by people in their day to day lives in five of our main provinces. Theirs are stories of laughter, loss, community, hope and fear - of a country often divided, but sometimes unexpectedly and joyfully united. Amplified by commentary which creates historical context, these are the stories of South Africa, three decades into freedom.

Watch the 90-minute Carte Blanche Special, 30 Years of Democracy on Sunday, 28 April at 7pm on M-Net (DStv Channel 101). Because of the extended duration, the Sunday night movie will start at 21:30 on the 28th. You can also live-stream it on DStv Stream, and watch on DStv Catch Up after the broadcast. Join the conversation on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook using the hashtag #CarteBlanche.

This is a story about South Africa and her people: A reflection on how we are doing, what brought us to this point and how do we feel about the future. Summary: The history of SA is one of migration, displacement, belonging, exile, leaving home to seek new opportunities elsewhere. So our focus will be on the landscape and the different challenges experienced by the citizens of five of our main provinces. We propose dividing the 72 minute documentary into six parts (of about 12 minutes each), with an introduction and conclusion making up one part, and five longer parts where we get to know people who have been part of the democratic journey in different areas of the country, but who we find in their homes. To develop a picture of that journey we propose to separate each part or segment with poetic visuals – drones, wide shots, close up shots, stills, time lapses – of transport infrastructure: roads, railways, runways, traffic, taxis, cars, aeroplanes, potholes, broken bridges, contrasting both the sophisticated infrastructure that works and that which is broken. The images will also speak to what binds us, what connects us to the landscape. Much of this will be without voice over or narrative and will paint a verbal picture. They will also provide a dynamic tension with the homes we visit. We will need to film in both rural and urban spaces, across five provinces - Gauteng, Eastern Cape, Western Cape, Kwazulu-Natal and maybe Northern Cape. In locating our characters at home, we will also, by default, highlight the issues of migration, and displacement, isolation, belonging, disillusionment, loss, hope and love which are also common in the country’s experience. The infrastructure segways will contribute to that effect. We propose a narrative voice to link the parts but will keep the wording sparse. It will be a voice to link and create context rather than an explaining voice. We will focus the interview on three main questions: 1) How are you feeling about South Africa as your home? 2) What events have happened to make you feel like that? 3) What are your hopes for the future South Africa? Those questions will be set in an interview which also asks them questions about who they are and how they live their life. The answers will be threaded through the documentary with broader context provided by political and social experts. The characters and experts selected will be given licence to answer in seriousness but also with humour. We hope to interview approximately three to four people and expert in each province, with some specifically identified for a slightly different Afrikaans version. Release: M-Net Explore 30 Years of Democracy with Carte Blanche M-Net celebrates Freedom Day with the broadcast of a 90-minuted Carte Blanche special, looking back at three decades of democracy in South Africa, on Sunday 28 April at 7pm. 30 Years of Democracy tells the story of South Africa and her people, from the moment democracy was attained, , reflecting on the journey so far and imagining what the perfect destination looks like. Thirty years after the country’s first free, fair, democratic election in 1994, the Carte Blanche team travels across South Africa to meet people from all walks of life, sharing their realities, hearing their dreams and listening intently to their hopes for the future. Rather than being a history of post-apartheid South Africa or apolitical assessment of South Africa’s destiny,, 30 Years of Democracy seeks to gain an understanding of how South Africans have experienced the last thirty years living in this country, how it has shaped their identity and whether they believe their hopes, wants and needs will be realised in the future “The Carte Blanche team takes to the highways, streets and back roads to speak to South Africans from all walks of life in their homes: from a Sandton chef to a rural chief, a Durban Street artist to a medical student, and a lawyer to a taxi boss,” says Waldimar Pelser, Channel Director: Premium Channels at MultiChoice. “We think we know South Africa because we live the everyday realities – but how often do we consider the lived experience of a wider cross-section of the country and seek to understand what people’s hopes for their country are?” The history of SA is one of migration, displacement, belonging, exile and leaving home to seek new opportunities elsewhere. It’s also one of resilience and solidarity. 30 Years of Democracy focuses on the landscape and the different challenges experienced by people in their day to day lives in five of our main provinces. Theirs are stories of laughter, loss, community, hope and fear - of a country often divided, but sometimes unexpectedly and joyfully united. Amplified by commentary which creates historical context, these are the stories of South Africa, three decades into freedom. Watch the 90-minute Carte Blanche Special, 30 Years of Democracy on Sunday, 28 April at 7pm on M-Net (DStv Channel 101). metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South Africans reflect on how the democratic South Africa has served them as their home over the last thirty years
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have a unique opportunity to feel the pulse of South Africa's democracy through the lived experience of a range of people across South Africa. This is a story about South Africa and her people: A reflection on how we are doing, what brought us to this point and how do we feel about the future.
metadata.Summary: The history of SA is one of migration, displacement, belonging, exile, leaving home to seek new opportunities elsewhere. So our focus will be on the landscape and the different challenges experienced by the citizens of five of our main provinces. We propose dividing the 72 minute documentary into six parts (of about 12 minutes each), with an introduction and conclusion making up one part, and five longer parts where we get to know people who have been part of the democratic journey in different areas of the country, but who we find in their homes. To develop a picture of that journey we propose to separate each part or segment with poetic visuals – drones, wide shots, close up shots, stills, time lapses – of transport infrastructure: roads, railways, runways, traffic, taxis, cars, aeroplanes, potholes, broken bridges, contrasting both the sophisticated infrastructure that works and that which is broken. The images will also speak to what binds us, what connects us to the landscape. Much of this will be without voice over or narrative and will paint a verbal picture. They will also provide a dynamic tension with the homes we visit. We will need to film in both rural and urban spaces, across five provinces - Gauteng, Eastern Cape, Western Cape, Kwazulu-Natal and maybe Northern Cape. In locating our characters at home, we will also, by default, highlight the issues of migration, and displacement, isolation, belonging, disillusionment, loss, hope and love which are also common in the country’s experience. The infrastructure segways will contribute to that effect. We propose a narrative voice to link the parts but will keep the wording sparse. It will be a voice to link and create context rather than an explaining voice. We will focus the interview on three main questions: 1) How are you feeling about South Africa as your home? 2) What events have happened to make you feel like that? 3) What are your hopes for the future South Africa? Those questions will be set in an interview which also asks them questions about who they are and how they live their life. The answers will be threaded through the documentary with broader context provided by political and social experts. The characters and experts selected will be given licence to answer in seriousness but also with humour. We hope to interview approximately three to four people and expert in each province, with some specifically identified for a slightly different Afrikaans version.
